statements: The chief complaint is a 6-week history of dull right upper-quadrant abdominal pain in a 26-year-old woman.
The woman has a known childhood diagnosis of mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver.
Her major clinical concern is a previously documented hepatic lesion that has enlarged and is now symptomatic in adulthood.
She had a 9 × 8 cm multiseptated cystic mass in the right hepatic lobe at 16 months of age.
The 9 × 8 cm multiseptated cystic mass was interpreted as mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver.
The lesion was never resected.
CT shows interval growth of the lesion to 12.9 × 8.3 cm.
The interval growth indicates persistence and enlargement over many years.
There is a new 6 cm peripheral enhancing region within the posterior aspect of the lesion.
MRI shows heterogeneous internal signal intensity.
FDG-PET shows focal hypermetabolism.
A benign mesenchymal hamartoma is typically predominantly cystic.
Development of a new enhancing solid component raises concern for malignant transformation.
Focal metabolic activity raises concern for malignant transformation.
Enlarged hepatoduodenal lymph nodes are present.
Enlarged portocaval lymph nodes are present.
The enlarged hepatoduodenal and portocaval lymph nodes support a neoplastic process rather than a stable benign hamartoma.
She now has right upper-quadrant pain.
She has mild right upper-quadrant tenderness.
CA 19-9 is markedly elevated at 1075 U/mL.
AFP is normal.
CEA is normal.
Liver enzymes are essentially normal.
GGT is minimally elevated.
Normal AFP argues against hepatoblastoma.
Normal AFP argues against conventional hepatocellular malignancy.
Normal CEA makes metastatic gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma less supported.
There is no mention of fever.
There is no mention of leukocytosis.
There is no mention of systemic inflammatory signs.
There is no mention of rebound.
There is no mention of guarding.
The absence of rebound or guarding makes an acute surgical abdomen unlikely.
The lesion was known since infancy.
The lesion being known since infancy makes a de novo adult primary cystic liver lesion less likely than evolution of the preexisting mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver.
The first candidate differential is persistent benign mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver.
This diagnosis fits the childhood diagnosis.
This diagnosis fits the long history of a multiseptated cystic right-lobe lesion.
Persistent benign mesenchymal hamartoma does not adequately explain the new 6 cm enhancing component.
Persistent benign mesenchymal hamartoma does not adequately explain focal FDG uptake.
Persistent benign mesenchymal hamartoma does not adequately explain enlarged regional lymph nodes.
Persistent benign mesenchymal hamartoma does not adequately explain marked CA 19-9 elevation.
These changes suggest that the lesion is no longer behaving as a purely benign hamartoma.
The next major differential is undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver arising in association with or transformation from mesenchymal hamartoma.
This diagnosis fits particularly well because mesenchymal hamartoma is a recognized precursor or associated lesion for undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver.
A longstanding cystic hepatic lesion that develops new solid enhancing areas in a young patient supports this diagnosis.
The heterogeneous MRI appearance supports this diagnosis.
Focal hypermetabolism on PET supports this diagnosis.
Interval growth supports this diagnosis.
Symptoms support this diagnosis.
Nodal enlargement supports this diagnosis.
Normal AFP is compatible with undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver.
Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver typically does not elevate AFP.
Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver is more common in children.
Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver can occur in young adults.
Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver is the classic malignant counterpart linked to mesenchymal hamartoma.
Another differential is intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arising within a cystic hepatic lesion.
Another differential is cystadenocarcinoma arising within a cystic hepatic lesion.
Markedly elevated CA 19-9 could suggest biliary malignancy.
An enhancing component within a cystic liver mass could suggest biliary malignancy.
The lesion’s origin in infancy as a mesenchymal hamartoma makes biliary malignancy less likely than sarcomatous transformation of the known mesenchymal hamartoma.
The patient is quite young for cholangiocarcinoma.
The overall clinical narrative is more consistent with malignant change in a congenital or childhood lesion.
Biliary cystadenoma could present as a multiloculated cystic hepatic mass.
Biliary cystadenocarcinoma could present as a multiloculated cystic hepatic mass.
Biliary cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma could present with elevated CA 19-9.
Biliary cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma could present with mural enhancement.
The documented diagnosis since infancy of mesenchymal hamartoma makes biliary cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma a less favored explanation.
The known association between mesenchymal hamartoma and undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma makes biliary cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma a less favored explanation.
The most likely diagnosis is malignant transformation of mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver into undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma.
The preexisting childhood mesenchymal hamartoma is a decisive feature.
Interval enlargement is a decisive feature.
Development of a new enhancing solid component is a decisive feature.
Heterogeneous MRI signal is a decisive feature.
Focal FDG uptake is a decisive feature.
Regional lymphadenopathy is a decisive feature.
New symptoms are a decisive feature.
Pathology would be required for definitive confirmation.
Among the diagnostic possibilities, malignant transformation of mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver into undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma is the single best fit to the provided data.
The differential diagnosis includes undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver arising in mesenchymal hamartoma.
The differential diagnosis includes persistent benign mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver.
The differential diagnosis includes biliary cystadenocarcinoma or intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arising in a cystic hepatic lesion.
The final diagnosis is undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver arising in mesenchymal hamartoma.
